name: Azazel
title: Azazel – the concept linked to the scapegoat on the Day of Atonement
summary: On the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), as described in Leviticus 16, Azazel plays a central role in one of the Old Testament's most significant rituals. The term designates the recipient of the goat that the high priest sent out into the wilderness after symbolically laying the people's sins upon its head. Azazel is not a biblical person in the traditional sense, but rather a debated ritual and theological concept. The very meaning of the word has been subject to extensive debate – interpretations range from 'the goat that disappears', through a supernatural desert figure, to a place name. During the Day of Atonement ritual, lots were cast over two goats: one was sacrificed to the Lord as a sin offering, and the other was sent away to Azazel in the wilderness. Together, the two goats express a complex picture of atonement – both a substitute sacrifice and the complete removal of sin from God's people. In Christian theological tradition, this ritual is understood as a foreshadowing of the atonement that Christ later accomplished.
roles: Ritual concept in the liturgy of the Day of Atonement
Central element in the Yom Kippur ritual
Typological foreshadowing of complete forgiveness of sins

keyEvents.title: The Day of Atonement ritual is established
keyEvents.description: God gives Moses instructions for the Day of Atonement, where two goats are to be chosen – one for the Lord and one for Azazel. The ritual establishes the framework for annual atonement for the people of Israel.

keyEvents.title: The casting of lots between the two goats
keyEvents.description: Aaron casts lots over the two goats at the entrance of the tent of meeting – one lot for the Lord and one for Azazel. The casting of lots emphasizes that the selection is in God's hand.

keyEvents.title: Sins are laid upon the Azazel goat
keyEvents.description: Aaron places both hands on the head of the live goat and confesses all Israel's sins and transgressions over it, symbolically laying them upon the goat's head.

keyEvents.title: The Goat Is Sent Out into the Wilderness
keyEvents.description: The goat for Azazel is sent out into the wilderness by a man appointed for this task, carrying all the people's sins away to a desolate land, as a symbol of the complete removal of sin from the community.

keyEvents.title: The Day of Atonement as an Everlasting Ordinance
keyEvents.description: The ritual with the Azazel goat is part of the annual Day of Atonement, established as an everlasting ordinance for the people of Israel to make atonement for all their sins.

keyEvents.title: Christ as the Fulfillment of the Atonement Ritual
keyEvents.description: The Letter to the Hebrews points to Christ as the final high priest who entered the Most Holy Place with his own blood once for all. Although the Azazel goat is not explicitly mentioned, the rituals of the Day of Atonement are understood in Christian tradition as shadowy images of Christ's perfect work of atonement.

versions.summary: Azazel is a term found in Leviticus in connection with the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur). It refers to the goat that was sent out into the wilderness bearing the people's sins, symbolizing the complete removal of sin. Azazel is not a person in the traditional sense but an important ritual and theological concept in the Old Testament, often interpreted as a wilderness spirit or symbolic recipient of the people's sins.
versions.title: The Scapegoat in the Wilderness
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Scapegoat in the Wilderness' is slightly imprecise. Azazel is not the goat itself, but the name or concept to which the goat is sent or for which it is designated. A more precise title would reflect that Azazel is the recipient or concept, not the goat itself.; [major] The roles array is empty. Although Azazel is not a person in the traditional sense, it should still contain relevant descriptions such as 'ritual concept', 'symbolic recipient of sin', or similar to give the profile substance.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. A complex and debated concept like Azazel deserves footnotes covering the linguistic debate over the word's meaning, rabbinic interpretations, its connection to the Book of 1 Enoch, and the theological typology linked to Christ.; [minor] The description mentions verse 20 in addition to verses 21–22, but verse 20 concerns the conclusion of atonement in the holy place, not directly the confession of sins over the goat. Verses 21–22 are the most central here.; [minor] The connection between the Azazel ritual and Hebrews is theologically sound, but it should be clarified that Hebrews primarily focuses on the blood sacrifice (the goat for the Lord) rather than specifically the Azazel goat. Nevertheless, the typology remains valid within a broader atonement context.; [minor] The summary is good, but the expression 'wilderness spirit' is only one of several interpretations and can be misleading without qualification. It should be noted that interpretations vary between 'a wilderness demon', 'a place name', 'complete removal' (from Hebrew ez + azel), and others.

The term refers to the goat that was sent out into the wilderness with the people's sins symbolically placed upon it, as an image of the complete removal of sin from the community. Azazel is not a person in the traditional sense, but an important ritual and theological concept in the Old Testament. The meaning of the word itself is debated – interpretations include 'the goat that disappears', a supernatural wilderness figure, or a place name. The two goats on the Day of Atonement – one sacrificed for the Lord and one sent to Azazel – together illustrate a complete picture of atonement: both a sin-bearing sacrifice and total removal of sin. In Christian theology this ritual is seen as a precursor to Christ's atoning work.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew word 'azazel' (עֲזָאזֵל) is disputed. The main interpretations include: (1) a compound word from 'ez' (goat) and 'azel' (to vanish), meaning 'the goat that vanishes'; (2) a proper name for a desert demon or supernatural being; (3) a place name for a steep cliff in the wilderness. The Septuagint translates it as 'apopompaios' (the one who sends away), supporting the interpretation of removal.

In rabbinic tradition (Mishnah, Yoma 6:1–8), it is described in detail how the Azazel goat was led out into the wilderness and thrown off a cliff called Tzuk in the desert. A red thread was tied to the goat's horns, and tradition says that if God had forgiven the people's sins, the thread turned white (cf. Isa 1:18).

In the First Book of Enoch (1 En 8–10), a Jewish pseudepigraphical work from the second century BCE, Azazel is portrayed as a fallen angel who taught humans warfare and vanity and was bound in the wilderness as punishment. This tradition may have influenced the Jewish understanding of the Azazel ritual as sending sin back to its origin.

The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) was the only day of the year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place. The two goats represented two aspects of atonement: one was sacrificed as a sin offering for the Lord (a substitutionary sacrifice), and the other symbolically carried away the people's sins into the wilderness (complete removal). Together they illustrate a complete picture of atonement.

Archaeological finds from the Second Temple period, including the Dead Sea Scrolls, show that the concept of Azazel was known and discussed in various Jewish communities. In the Temple Scroll and other Qumran texts, there are references to the rituals of the Day of Atonement confirming its central role in Jewish practice.

Parallels to the scapegoat ritual have been found in other ancient cultures of the Middle East. Hittite ritual texts describe similar practices where an animal was burdened with impurity or a curse and sent away from the community. This suggests that the concept was known in the broader cultural context, but in Israelite religion it was framed within a unique monotheistic theology of atonement.
